description: Leccinum scabrum (Brown Birch Bolete) is a birch-associated ectomycorrhizal bolete with a tan to grey-brown cap, whitish pores, and a pale stem covered in dark scabers. The soft flesh may darken on cutting and turns blackish on cooking. Edible only when thoroughly cooked; of modest culinary quality.
edibilityNotes: Edible ONLY when thoroughly cooked. Raw or undercooked boletes of this group can cause gastrointestinal upset, so always cook well before eating. The flesh is soft and mild; older specimens become spongy and waterlogged and are best discarded or used only for drying. Within the scaber-stalk (Leccinum) complex, several segregate species are difficult to separate; L. scabrum itself is regarded as a safe edible but is unremarkable in flavour. As with any wild fungus, identify with certainty and eat only a small portion when trying a species for the first time.
distribution: Widespread across the temperate Northern Hemisphere, including Europe, the Himalayas, northern Asia, and North America, wherever birch occurs; also introduced with planted birch in parts of the Southern Hemisphere (notably Australia and New Zealand).

dangerousLookalikes.name: Other Leccinum scaber-stalks (e.g. Leccinum variicolor, Leccinum holopus, Leccinum oxydabile)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Closely related birch-associated scaber stalks, also edible-when-cooked, separated by cap colour, flesh staining (e.g. blue-green stipe base in L. variicolor) and habitat. Not dangerous, but the group is a complex rather than a single clean species; all require thorough cooking.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Tylopilus felleus (Bitter Bolete)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Superficially bolete-like with a brown cap, but has a coarse dark net (reticulation) on the stem rather than discrete scabers, pores that flush pinkish with age, and an intensely bitter taste that ruins a dish. Not deadly but renders food inedible.
